nameStory: Apple mint gets its delightful name from its sweet, fruity fragrance that smells remarkably like fresh apples when you crush the leaves. Unlike other mints that can be sharp or medicinal-smelling, this one has a mellow, almost dessert-like aroma. It's also called woolly mint because of its distinctively fuzzy, soft leaves that feel like velvet between your fingers.
description: Apple mint is a fuzzy-leaved perennial herb that grows 1-3 feet tall in upright clumps. Its most distinctive features are the soft, woolly leaves that feel like velvet and smell sweetly of apples when crushed. The plant produces small white or pale pink flowers in dense spikes during summer, and like all mints, it has that characteristic square stem that you can feel when you roll it between your fingers.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Rounded, wrinkled leaves covered in soft, woolly hairs that make them feel like velvet - crush one and smell the sweet apple fragrance

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or pale pink flowers clustered in dense, cone-shaped spikes at the stem tips during summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Square stems that spread by underground runners, forming patches 1-3 feet tall with an upright, bushy appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, with deeply wrinkled surfaces and scalloped or toothed edges

habitat: Apple mint thrives in moist, rich soils and is commonly found in gardens, along stream banks, and in partially shaded areas. It prefers spots with consistent moisture and can tolerate both sun and light shade. As an introduced species from Europe, it's most often encountered as an escape from cultivation near old homesites or in disturbed areas.

seasonality.spring: New fuzzy leaves emerge early, already showing their distinctive woolly texture and apple scent when crushed.
seasonality.summer: Peak identification time with full foliage and white flower spikes blooming from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may yellow but often persist late into the season, still retaining their woolly texture and fragrance.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, but underground runners survive to sprout again in spring.

funFact: Apple mint is actually sterile and rarely produces viable seeds - instead, it spreads entirely through underground runners, meaning every patch you find is essentially one giant clone that could theoretically be hundreds of years old!
confusionNotes: Apple mint's woolly leaves make it easy to distinguish from other mints, which have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves. If you're unsure, just feel the leaves - apple mint feels like soft velvet, while spearmint and other common mints feel smooth and crisp.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "apple mint," it's not related to apple trees at all - the name comes purely from its apple-like fragrance. This European native has been cultivated in gardens for centuries and often persists long after the original gardens have disappeared.
compareHints: Among New England's mints, apple mint stands out immediately for its fuzzy, rounded leaves that feel like velvet. Spearmint has smooth, pointed leaves with a sharp minty smell, while Canada mint has narrower leaves and grows in wetter areas. The woolly texture is your best clue - no other mint in our region feels quite so soft and velvety.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canada mint differs from its relatives by having flowers clustered in the leaf joints rather than in terminal spikes like spearmint, and it's strictly a wetland plant while corn mint tolerates drier soils.
Spearmint differs from other New England mints by its nearly hairless leaves and sweet, mild fragrance.
Unlike spearmint and peppermint which form terminal flower spikes, corn mint's flowers cluster in whorls around the stem at leaf joints.
Unlike Canada mint which prefers moist but not waterlogged soils, watermint truly loves having wet feet and grows right at the water's edge.
Horse mint differs from our common native Canada mint by being much taller and having woolly-white stems rather than smooth ones.
